title: Run-Length Encoding

statement.md: Tick data compresses well because prices repeat: the simplest scheme is run-length encoding, replacing each maximal run of a repeated character with the character and its count. Encode a string as `char count` pairs, space-separated.

inputFormat: A single line string $s$ of lowercase letters, $1 \le |s| \le 10^6$.
outputFormat: Space-separated `char count` tokens for each maximal run, in order.
constraints: read the whole line (it may not end with a newline)

examples.explanation: Runs: aaa, bbb, cc, z, a — runs are maximal, so the two a-runs stay separate.

hints: Two indices: i at the start of a run, j advanced while the character matches.
A run of length 1 still emits `c1`.

editorial.md: Single left-to-right scan with two pointers: `i` anchors the current run, `j` walks to the end of it, emit `(s[i], j-i)`, set `i = j`. O(n) time, O(number of runs) output. The specification details that separate correct from almost-correct: length-1 runs still print, and identical runs separated by anything else are distinct (maximality).

Why this problem earns its place next to Huffman and delta encoding in a quant curriculum: time-series compression is a daily reality at tick granularity (billions of messages/day), and RLE-delta hybrids (run lengths of repeated deltas) are what real tick stores approximate. The skill being drilled is exact, careful scanning — the same discipline P&L parsers need.

solutions.python:
import sys
s = sys.stdin.read().strip()
out = []
i = 0
while i < len(s):
    j = i
    while j < len(s) and s[j] == s[i]: j += 1
    out.append(f"{s[i]}{j-i}")
    i = j
print(" ".join(out))

tests.expected: a1 b1 a1 b1 a1 b1
